circadian.title: Your circadian rhythm.
circadian.intro: The key to mastering your sleep schedule (or jet lag) is understanding that your circadian rhythm is... actually two things! They work together to make you sleepy or sleepless.
circadian.biologicalClock: Your biological clock. If the time you go to sleep and wake up is relatively consistent, your biological clock will make you feel more or less alert in a predictable way. If you usually wake up at 7:00 am and go to sleep at 10:00 pm, your biological clock will make you feel alert around 7:00 am and less alert around 10:00 pm. But your biological clock alone usually can't put you to sleep. You will need your sleep pressure too.
circadian.sleepPressure: Your sleep pressure builds up as you spend more time being awake. Usually, we start to feel tired after staying awake for 16 consecutive hours. Sleep pressure is kind of like a battery that runs out. This is why after a late night and sleep-in, you might feel like you can't fall asleep at your usual bedtime. You haven't been awake for a long enough time to build up your sleep pressure, so a dip in alertness isn't enough to put you asleep. It's hard to fall asleep when you still have 50% of your battery left.
circadian.batteryAnalogy: So, your sleep pressure and your biological clock work kind of like a battery and a charger. For you to power off, you need to have a near-empty battery and the charger unplugged. Your biological clock controls the time to pull the plug, but it only gives your a small time window before starting to charge again over your usual sleep time. This is why you tend to feel less sleepy as you pass your usual bedtime (at least for a while).
circadian.adjustment: Hmmm... But what if you start waking up at 11:00 am and going to sleep at 3:00 am? Your biological clock will adjust to make you feel alert around 11:00 am and sleepy around 3:00 am. It really doesn't care about the objective time of day. It's all about your personal time of day. That's why after a while, you'll notice it's tough to fall asleep at 11 pm again; biological clock thinks 11 pm is just the beginning of your evening. Time to pArTay!

bedtime.title: Bed time planning
bedtime.paragraph1: Moving your bedtime (and wake time) by 30 minutes a day is a conservative pace — the fastest phase shift achievable with an optimally-timed combination of light, schedule, and melatonin tops out around 1 hour a day, and advances are generally harder to achieve than delays. Staying at 30 minutes a day keeps the plan comfortably inside that ceiling, which is the safer direction to err.
bedtime.paragraph2: On its own, a prescribed sleep/wake schedule like this one hasn't been independently shown to shift your circadian clock — the clinical evidence is strongest for light exposure. So think of this schedule as the scaffold that the bright light (and, if enabled, melatonin) steps work through, rather than a treatment by itself.

light.title: Bright light exposure
light.paragraph1: Light is the best-evidenced lever in this plan. Morning light after your target wake time helps shift your clock earlier; light in the evening, before bedtime, helps shift it later — we pick the direction automatically based on whether your plan is an advance or a delay.
light.paragraph2: For an earlier (advance) plan, morning light also means keeping the few hours before bedtime relatively dim, since evening light works against the shift you're going for. For a later (delay) plan, avoiding light right after your old wake time matters at least as much as getting evening light.
light.paragraph3: If your plan is mainly about getting more sleep opportunity rather than shifting your clock, morning light is still useful — just for alertness, not as a clock-shifting signal.

chronobiotics.title: Chronobiotics
chronobiotics.paragraph1: Melatonin timing differs depending on whether you're shifting your schedule earlier, later, or mainly need more sleep opportunity — we pick the general approach that matches your plan.
chronobiotics.paragraph2: If your goal is mainly more sleep rather than a clock shift, a consistent bedtime, a dark and cool room, and cutting morning light/noise usually matter more than melatonin does, which is why we treat it as optional in that case.
chronobiotics.paragraph3: This isn't a personal dosing recommendation, and it isn't a substitute for talking to a clinician, especially if you're pregnant, on other medications, or have a health condition. Full citations are pending an in-progress science review.
